title: 1 Chronicles 23:24–32
context: The chapter closes by describing the Levites counted from twenty years old and upward, grounded in David’s words that the LORD has given rest to his people and dwells in Jerusalem, so the Levites no longer need to carry the tabernacle. Their duties now center on assisting the sons of Aaron in the courts and rooms, purifying holy things, preparing the show bread and meal offerings, keeping measures, offering praise morning and evening, and serving at the burnt offerings on Sabbaths, new moons, and set feasts. The shift from thirty years in 23:3 to twenty years here is stated by the text itself, which links it to David’s last words, without further explanation. Arminian and Reformed readers commonly read the passage as shared ground about faithful service in ordinary tasks and the place of daily praise in the life of God’s people. Both traditions commonly see the priestly service as a shadow fulfilled in Christ (compare Hebrews 8:5; 10:11), while honoring the Levites’ work in its own setting.

verses.text: These were the sons of Levi after their fathers’ houses, even the heads of the fathers’ houses of those who were counted individually, in the number of names by their polls, who did the work for the service of the LORD’s house, from twenty years old and upward.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the Levites counted from twenty years old and upward for service in the LORD’s house. The text itself records a different age from verse 3.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the adjustment as connected to new circumstances, which the following verses explain. Both traditions commonly leave the relationship between the figures unresolved, as the text does.

verses.text: For David said, “The LORD, the God of Israel, has given rest to his people; and he dwells in Jerusalem forever.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see David declaring that the LORD has given rest to his people and dwells in Jerusalem forever. Rest brings new forms of service.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the rest as God’s gift that prepares for the temple (compare 1 Chronicles 22:9; 2 Samuel 7:1). Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as celebrating God’s faithfulness to his promises.

verses.text: Also the Levites will no longer need to carry the tabernacle and all its vessels for its service.”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that the Levites no longer need to carry the tabernacle and its vessels. Their tasks change as God’s people settle.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the change as a transition from wilderness worship to temple worship. Both traditions commonly read the verse as showing that forms of service can change while the call to serve remains.

verses.text: For by the last words of David the sons of Levi were counted, from twenty years old and upward.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the Levites counted from twenty years old by David’s last words. The change is tied to David’s final instructions.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see David’s authority in ordering worship as part of his role as king under God. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as explaining the new age figure without resolving every question.

verses.text: For their duty was to wait on the sons of Aaron for the service of the LORD’s house—in the courts, in the rooms, and in the purifying of all holy things, even the work of the service of God’s house;
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the Levites assisting the sons of Aaron in the courts, rooms, and purifying of holy things. Supporting roles matter in worship.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see their service as essential to the priests’ work, though distinct from it (compare Numbers 3:9). Both traditions commonly honor the dignity of ordinary service in God’s house.

verses.text: for the show bread also, and for the fine flour for a meal offering, whether of unleavened wafers, or of that which is baked in the pan, or of that which is soaked, and for all measurements of quantity and size;
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the Levites handling the show bread, meal offerings, and measurements. Careful attention to detail is part of faithful service.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the precise duties as reflecting God’s concern for order in worship (compare Leviticus 24:8). Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as valuing diligence in small tasks (compare Colossians 3:23).

verses.text: and to stand every morning to thank and praise the LORD, and likewise in the evening;
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the Levites standing every morning and evening to thank and praise the LORD. Daily praise frames the life of worship.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the rhythm of praise as a model for the Christian life (compare Psalm 92:2; Hebrews 13:15). Both traditions commonly read the verse as calling for regular, grateful worship.

verses.text: and to offer all burnt offerings to the LORD on the Sabbaths, on the new moons, and on the set feasts, in number according to the ordinance concerning them, continually before the LORD;
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the Levites assisting at burnt offerings on Sabbaths, new moons, and feasts. Worship follows the rhythm God appointed.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the appointed times as part of the covenant order now fulfilled in Christ (compare Numbers 28:9; Hebrews 10:11). Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as showing that worship is ordered by God.

verses.text: and that they should keep the duty of the Tent of Meeting, the duty of the holy place, and the duty of the sons of Aaron their brothers for the service of the LORD’s house.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the Levites keeping the duties of the Tent of Meeting, the holy place, and their brothers the sons of Aaron. Faithful service supports the whole worship of Israel.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see their duty as guarding the holiness of God’s dwelling. Both traditions commonly read the verse as a summary of humble, faithful service.
